stories.headline: Messi tracker: Goals, assists, key moments in 2026
stories.summary: ESPN provides game-by-game analysis of Lionel Messi's performances for Inter Miami and Argentina.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi will aim for more success in 2026. His Inter Miami side captured its first MLS Cup title last season and will look to defend it -- and add further silverware too -- in its first season at Nu Stadium, the club's new home.

Messi also captained Argentina as they fell just one step short of defending their FIFA World Cup crown, losing 1-0 in extra time to Spain in the final of what could be his last tournament.

As the 39-year-old continues to feature for both club and country, ESPN will track his performances game-by-game, providing stats and analysis each time he pulls on a Herons or Albiceleste jersey.

Messi's 2026 tally:

Games played: 40
Goals: 36
Assists: 17

Oct. 6: Argentina 3-0 Benin

It was an emotionally charged night in Buenos Aires as Messi played his final international match for Argentina, the team that he had led to World Cup glory and two Copa América titles as captain.

The friendly match at the Estadio Monumental was goalless at halftime, but just a few minutes after the break Messi's in-swinging corner from the left was rattled home on the volley by Nicolás Otamendi.

Then, on the hour mark, Messi spotted Nico Paz in space 25 yards from goal. He fed a square pass with the outside of his boot to the Como player, who curled in a classy finish.

But the night undoubtedly belonged to Messi, and he fired a penalty into the top corner to cap off his 208th and final senior appearance for his country with his 126th goal.

Sep. 27: Columbus Crew 2-1 Inter Miami

Before heading to Argentina for his final international match, Messi gave Miami fans something to savor in Ohio.

From a set piece wide on the right wing and with most of those in the stadium, including those in the Columbus defense, surely expecting a cross, Messi's left foot sent the ball curling wickedly into the far top corner of the net.

Messi had chances to add to that tally in the second half but was denied from distance by Columbus goalkeeper Patrick Schulte and put another effort into the side netting.

Then Jamal Thiaré scored in the eighth minute of second-half stoppage time to give the Columbus Crew a stunning 2-1 win.

Sep. 20: Inter Miami 2-2 San Diego FC

Messi's sublime curling free kick was not enough to inspire the Herons to a win against San Diego on Sunday night.

After falling behind to an Anders Dreyer goal in the 12th minute, 39-year-old Messi levelled the scores with beautiful set-piece shot in the 24th minute. His well-hit effort evaded a number of attackers and defenders before sneaking in at the far post.

Miami thought they'd won the match after Luiz Suarez fired the hosts ahead in the 74th minute, only for Dreyer to nab his second goal of the game and ensure the points were shared.

Sep. 16: Inter Miami 2-0 Cruz Azul

Another day, another trophy for Messi.

The Argentine master scored his 100th goal for Inter Miami as the Herons defeated Cruz Azul 2-0 on Wednesday night to win the Campeones Cup.

Messi opened the scoring in the 24th minute, heading in a cross from Luis Suárez, before turning provider for Casemiro -- sending in a corner for the Brazilian to nod home.

Sep. 12: Inter Miami 2-2 Nashville SC
In a matchup between the two best teams in the Eastern Conference, the action went end to end, with Messi getting on the scoresheet for Miami's second goal off a Rodrigo De Paul assist as he continues to lead the Golden Boot race.

Ultimately, the teams settled for a point apiece, as the hosts failed to close the gap on Nashville at the top of the table.

Sep. 9: Chicago Fire 1-1 Inter Miami

Two or Europe's greatest club players took center stage in one of the United States' most iconic American football stadiums on Wednesday -- and a record crowd came out to watch.

Ex-Bayern Munich and Barcelona star Robert Lewandowski scored a trademark acrobatic goal in the 10th minute to give the Fire an early lead at the NFL home of the Chicago Bears.

But Inter Miami drew level shortly after halftime when Casemiro, another of the game's stars with a long history of playing in Europe before moving to MLS, headed home a Messi cross from a corner kick to make it 1-1.

The assist was Messi's league-leading 13th of the season. He also has league 18 goals and is the first player in MLS history with 30-plus goal contributions in three separate seasons.

Sep. 5: Inter Miami 2-2 Atlanta United
Messi was not as effective as he was in the previous matchup, but he did get an assist for Casemiro's opening goal. However, his team was unable to win as they had to settle for a point in a 2-2 draw.

August 29: Inter Miami 7-1 CF Montréal

Fans were treated to a Messi masterclass on Saturday as the Argentine magician registered four goals and an assist to help Miami to a club-record 7-1 victory over CF Montréal.

Messi scored with a deflected free kick in the 40th minute before netting after a stunning solo run in the 52nd. After supplying an assist to Luis Suárez, the 39-year-old then completed his hat trick and with a delicate chip over the goalkeeper with seven minutes of regulation time remaining.

He wasn't done yet.

Deep into stoppage time, Messi lined up a free kick and dispatched it with trademark precision into the top corner of the net. Legendary stuff.

August 22: Inter Miami 2-1 Toronto FC

Messi's 14th MLS goal of the season wasn't enough to prevent Inter Miami from slumping to their fourth loss in their last five games, losing 2-1 to Toronto FC at Nu Stadium on Saturday.

Messi found the net with a first-time finish from a Rodrigo De Paul through-ball with eight minutes remaining, but the home side's late rally fell short of salvaging a much-needed draw to bolster the Herons' pursuit of first-placed Nashville SC in the Eastern Conference.

August 19: Inter Miami 2-2 Philadelphia Union

Messi is back scoring goals, but unfortunately, his Miami side is not back to winning ways. The Argentine scored Miami's second goal of the night as both teams finished with 10 men. Miami are now winless in their last four matches.

August 15: Nashville SC 4-1 Inter Miami
It was not the best night for Messi in Tennessee. The Argentine missed yet another penalty -- his third straight for club and country -- and they suffered a heavy 4-1 loss to their Eastern Conference rivals. However, he did get an assist for Telasco Segovia's equalizer at halftime before Miami lost control in the second half.

August 12: Inter Miami 2-3 Club León
Just days after the passing of his father, Messi came off the bench in the second half to try to help Miami continue in the Leagues Cup after they were leading 1-0. However, it ended in a 3-2 loss which saw them eliminated in the league phase after a second straight loss, coming off defeat to Monterrey last weekend with Messi away at the memorial for his father.

August 5: Inter Miami 4-2 Atlético de San Luis

Lionel Messi made his first start for Inter Miami since returning from the World Cup and picked up right where he left off, scoring a stellar pair of goals to guide his team to a come-from-behind 4-2 rout of Atlético de San Luis in its first game of the 2026 Leagues Cup.

Messi's first goal was an exquisite volley, redirecting Noah Allen's cross from the left flank while running at full speed. Miami's third goal of the opening half -- and Messi's second on the night -- came on the back of some intricate buildup play with Allen once again setting up his team captain, this time in the center of the area where he tiptoed through two defenders and buried a close-range strike past Andrés Sánchez.

The goal made Messi the all-time leading scorer in Leagues Cup history with 14, one ahead of LAFC's Denis Bouanga since the expanded competition began in 2023.

August 1: Inter Miami 2-2 Columbus Crew
Messi made his return to action for Inter Miami on Saturday, 13 days after tasting defeat with Argentina in the World Cup final. The Miami talisman started on the substitutes' bench before being introduced in the 53rd minute of the Herons' 2-2 draw with the Columbus Crew at Nu Stadium in Miami.

July 19: Spain 1-0 AET Argentina

Sunday proved to be a bridge too far for both Messi and Argentina, falling in extra time to Spain in the World Cup final.

With La Roja controlling the match basically from start to finish -- Argentina didn't register a shot on target during regulation time -- Messi had few opportunities to impact the game. Indeed, the 39-year-old was given a 3/10 in ESPN's post-match player ratings.

Still, as Mark Ogden points out, the 2026 tournament was a memorable one for Messi and cemented his status as the GOAT, if it were ever in doubt.

July 15: England 1-2 Argentina
Messi made another statement in his 205th appearance for Argentina, this time in his first-ever match against England in a World Cup semifinal. With so much at stake for both nations, Messi once again proved decisive despite not getting on the scoresheet.

He first provided the assist for Enzo Fernández's superb strike to level the match in the second half before delivering a pinpoint cross for Lautaro Martínez's headed winner, sending the reigning champions into yet another World Cup final after another dramatic encounter.

Messi has now recorded either a goal or an assist in all seven of Argentina's matches at this World Cup, and he will have the opportunity to lift the trophy for a second time when Argentina face Spain in Sunday's final in New Jersey.

July 11: Argentina 3-1 Switzerland
It was a relatively quiet night by Messi's standards as his goalscoring streak came to an end, but his influence on the match stayed the same. He set up Alexis Mac Allister's opening goal for Argentina against Switzerland, and although the match went to extra time, the defending champions won 3-1 thanks to two late goals in the second half of extra time.

Messi's quest to retain the World Cup now continues into the semifinals, where Argentina will face England for the first time in over 20 years. The clash in Atlanta -- one of international soccer's most storied rivalries -- will decide a spot in the final.

July 7: Argentina 3-2 Egypt
It was another dramatic outing for Messi and Argentina, who rallied from a 2-0 deficit to defeat Egypt 3-2 in Atlanta and book their place in the World Cup quarterfinals. As is so often the case, Messi was at the center of the action. Minutes after Egypt opened the scoring, he missed another penalty, but he quickly made amends by setting up Cristian Romero for Argentina's first goal. Messi then scored the equalizer -- his eighth goal of the tournament -- before Enzo Fernández completed the comeback with the winner. Argentina will now face Switzerland in Kansas City for a place in the semifinals.

July 3: Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde
Messi suffered a major scare in Miami Gardens on Friday evening in the round of 32, but it ultimately ended well for Argentina. He opened the scoring with his seventh goal of the tournament, extending his World Cup tally to 20 goals while finding the net in a record eighth consecutive World Cup match. Cape Verde twice fought back -- once in the second half and again in extra time -- but the world champions eventually prevailed 3-2 after extra time to book a meeting in the round of 16 with Egypt.

June 27: Jordan 1-3 Argentina
Messi didn't play the full 90 minutes in Argentina's 3-1 win over an already-eliminated Jordan, but he still made his mark during a 30-minute cameo in Texas. The 39-year-old scored a free kick for his sixth goal of the tournament and his 19th career World Cup goal, becoming the first player ever to score in seven consecutive World Cup matches. Even at 39, he's still got it.

June 22: Argentina 2-0 Austria
Another chapter in an already unparalleled career. Lionel Messi scored twice in Argentina's 2-0 win over Austria to help his team qualify for the round of 32 and become the outright leading goalscorer in men's and women's FIFA World Cup history with 18 goals. After missing an early penalty, he responded by breaking Miroslav Klose's 12-year-old record and then added a second late on to break Marta's record. All just two days before turning 39.

June 16: Argentina 3-0 Algeria
In his 200th appearance for Argentina and sixth World Cup, Lionel Messi sent a message to the world just days before his 39th birthday: he still has it. His first-ever World Cup hat trick powered Argentina to victory in their group-stage opener, while his 16th tournament goal saw him draw level with Miroslav Klose for the most goals in World Cup history.

June 9: Argentina 3-0 Iceland

Messi, working his way back from muscle fatigue ahead of the start of the World Cup, came on in the 70th minute of a pre-tournament friendly in Auburn, Alabama and scored from the penalty spot right afterward.

It was Messi's 911th career goal for club and country and 117th goal for Argentina and made him the oldest scorer in the country's soccer history.

May 24: Inter Miami 6-4 Philadelphia Union

Messi registered two assists in a scintillating performance against Philadelphia on Sunday but, unfortunately, no one was focused on results come the end of the game.

That's because, in the very last game before the World Cup, Messi left the field in the 73rd minute and headed straight to the locker room after grabbing his left thigh.

Now, supporters around the world are holding their collective breath while they wait and see if the injury has scuppered the 38-year-old's chance of appearing at a sixth World Cup.

May 13: FC Cincinnati 3-5 Inter Miami

Two goals and one assist marked yet another spectacular contribution from Miami superstar Messi on Wednesday. The Argentine magician was instrumental as the Herons fought back from 3-2 down to eventually beat Cincinnati 5-3 at TQL Stadium in Ohio.

May 9: Toronto FC 2-4 Inter Miami

It was a day of star power. Not only were Rodrigo De Paul, Luis Suárez and Sergio Reguilón all on the score sheet for the Herons, so was Messi -- and he added a pair of assists, too.

While Miami has yet to taste victory at its new home, it continues to take care of business on the road. Saturday's win in Toronto extended the club's unbeaten record away from home in 2026 to seven games, picking up six wins and one draw in the first few months of the season.

May 2: Inter Miami 3-4 Orlando City

Messi notched a goal and an assist on Saturday in what ended up being an astonishing collapse for Inter Miami at Nu Stadium.

The Herons were leading 3-0 after Messi's classy 33rd-minute strike, but gifted the visitors four goals -- including a Martín Ojeda hat trick -- to once again miss out on a victory at their new home ground. Orlando's comeback from three goals down marks only the third time in MLS history that a team has claimed all three points after trailing by three or more goals.

As for Messi's Miami, only twice has an MLS team had a longer winless run -- now up to four for the Herons -- to open up a new stadium.

April 25: Inter Miami 1-1 New England Revolution
Messi again failed to get on the scoresheet as Miami put in a fatigued second-half performance that saw them come from a goal down against New England. It was another draw -- and another game without a win at their new home, Nu Stadium.

April 22: Real Salt Lake 0-2 Inter Miami
No goals or assists from Messi as Miami visited America First Field on Wednesday, but the fans did get treated to sumptuous strikes nonetheless.

Rodrigo De Paul's opener in the 80th-minute was stunning curler from outside the box and then, almost immediately after the restart, Luis Suarez made it 2-0 with a well-struck volley.

The victory moves Inter Miami into outright second in the MLS Eastern Conference.

April 18: Colorado Rapids 2-3 Inter Miami

Another moment of Messi magic bagged all three points for Inter Miami on Saturday.

With scores level in the 79th minute, the Argentine icon danced his way past a number of Colorado defenders before curling home an outrageous effort into the far corner.

The strike -- Messi's second of the match after converting a penalty in the first half -- helped Miami to their first win under interim coach Guillermo Hoyos.

Hoyos, who had been serving as club's sporting director, took over coaching duties after Javier Mascherano unexpectedly left the club due to personal reasons last week.

April 11: Inter Miami 2-2 Red Bull New York
Miami and Messi are still waiting for a first win at Nu Stadium after a 2-2 draw with Red Bull New York on Saturday night.

Messi didn't register a goal or assist, but did help set up Germán Berterame's second-half strike that gave Inter Miami its first lead at its new home ground, but 17-year-old Adri Mehmeti's first career goal in the 77th minute secured a point for the visitors.

April 4: Inter Miami 2-2 Austin FC
Inter Miami opened Nu Stadium the only way it knows how: With a Messi goal. The No. 10 began the move in trademark style with a left-footed pass to a teammate before moving past a defender and arriving in the box at just the right time to head past goalkeeper Brad Stuver.

March 31: Argentina 5-0 Zambia
It was the last day of the month and perhaps the last game for Messi playing for Argentina playing in his native country, but they put on a show defeating the African side Zambia 5-0. Messi scored the second goal for Lionel Scaloni's side as focus will shift now to Miami until the beginning of the World Cup.

March 27: Argentina 2-1 Mauritania
In his first game for his country in 2026, Messi only played the second half as Argentina won 2-1 against Mauritania at the mythical La Bombonera in Buenos Aires, as the World Cup champions continue to prepare to defend their title this summer in North America.

March 22: NYCFC 2-3 Inter Miami

It was a thrilling encounter in the Bronx, as the Argentine star helped his team to a 3-2 win over NYCFC, which also included another trademark free kick goal, now beginning his course for potentially 1,000 career goals. Only 99 goals left!

March 18: Inter Miami 1-1 Nashville SC

Messi may have made history on Wednesday night, becoming just the second men's player in history to score 900 career goals, but it wasn't enough to seal Miami's progress in the Concacaf Champions Cup.

The Argentina legend found the back of the net in the seventh minute at Chase Stadium, but his strike was cancelled out by Nashville's Cristian Espinoza -- sealing the Herons' tournament exit on the away goals rule.

March 11: Nashville SC 0-0 Inter Miami
A drab night for Messi and Co. in the Concacaf Champions Cup. Plenty of possession but few shots on target mean that the Herons will return to Chase Stadium know a win will be needed to ensure progression.

March 7: D.C. United 1-2 Inter Miami

It was quite an eventful week for Messi. Just days before Miami's match against D.C. United, Messi and the entire squad visited the White House and met President Donald Trump and were eager to put on a show for the sold-out crowd of over 70,000 at Baltimore's M&T Bank Stadium.

And they did just that, with a 2-1 win over D.C. United. Messi, of course, scored Miami's second and is now one goal away from 900 career goals.

March 1: Orlando City 2-4 Inter Miami

Well, that blip didn't last long! Messi and Miami roared back into life with a 4-2 thrashing of Orlando on Sunday thanks to the 38-year-old's wizardry.

Things looked ominous for the Herons after the first 45 minutes, down 2-0 and looking on course to start the MLS season with two bleak losses.

But two goals and an assist from Messi in the second half dragged the visitors back in the game and helped secure Miami their first points of the season.

Feb. 21: LAFC 3-0 Inter Miami
Messi and Miami aimed to start 2026 firing on all cylinders, but it was the hosts who spoiled the defending MLS Cup champions' opener at the LA Coliseum. In front of a sellout crowd of 75,673 -- the second-highest attendance in MLS history -- Miami were outplayed, with LAFC's Denis Bouanga getting a goal and an assist in a convincing home victory.

The main talking point, however, emerged after the final whistle. Messi was initially reported to have gained unauthorized access to the officials' locker room after video circulated showing him near the area. However, it was later reported that no league policy had been violated and Messi was cleared of any wrongdoing. Miami will now turn its attention next weekend against fellow Florida side Orlando City.

stories.headline: Mercedes confirm George Russell engine penalty at Singapore Grand Prix
stories.summary: Mercedes has confirmed that George Russell will serve an engine penalty at the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday.
stories.body:
Mercedes has confirmed George Russell will start from the back of the grid at Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix due to an engine penalty.

Russell retired from third at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia due to a power unit failure with six laps remaining.

Mercedes need to introduce replacement power unit to Russell's car in Singapore, which will take him above his quota of power unit components for the season and result in a back-of-the-grid penalty.

It is another setback to his championship hopes. His teammate Kimi Antonelli's lead at the top of the F1 standings sits at 84 points, and Russell is second.

Team principal Toto Wolff's pre-race statement said: "George has the added challenge of a power unit penalty [in Singapore], which will mean starting from the back of the grid on Sunday, following the engine failure in Malaysia.

"That is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for. Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."

After reliability issues earlier this year, Mercedes was already planning for Russell to take an additional power unit and the resulting penalty before the end of the season, but was not expecting to do so in Singapore where overtaking in the race is notoriously difficult.

The failure in Malaysia forced the team's hand as Russell does not have enough low-mileage components in his pool of engine parts to avoid taking a new power unit this weekend.

The situation is further complicated for Russell as Mercedes was planning to bring a performance upgrade to its power unit at the U.S. Grand Prix in two weeks' time, which the team had hoped would coincide with the introduction of Russell's final power unit of the year.

Mercedes has not yet confirmed whether the upgrade can be fast-tracked for introduction in Singapore or whether Russell will need to use older specification parts this weekend.

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord warned in Malaysia that Russell may face a "double whammy" if he then has to take another penalty at the U.S. Grand Prix to access the upgraded power unit for the rest of the season.

Wolff also confirmed that his team will use this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix to assess the aerodynamic upgrades it brought to its car in Malaysia.

Despite expectations that the update would move the championship leaders comfortably ahead of its competitors, Max Verstappen's Red Bull proved to be fastest car at Sepang while Mercedes was left scratching its head over its relative lack of performance.

Wolff revealed his team would use the Singapore weekend to run direct comparisons between its previous aerodynamic package and the new updates.

"Malaysia was obviously a very difficult weekend for us," Wolff said. "We have spent the days since then working hard to understand why our performance was not where it should have been.

"We have identified several areas we need to investigate further, but F1 doesn't offer simple answers and we need more evidence before drawing firm conclusions.

"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work. The characteristics of the circuit are very different and that will help us build a clearer picture of where we are.

"That is why we will evaluate both the latest update package and our previous specification across the weekend to ensure we fully understand the direction we need to take."

stories.headline: Matchmaking, inactivity -- and, yes, fights -- shift MMA divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
The fighter who won a UFC championship on Saturday does not move an inch in the ESPN divisional rankings. But several other fighters who did not even compete over the weekend do rise in their divisions' top 10s. One shifts from the top of one division's rankings to the middle of the pack in another weight class.

The new champion is Natalia Silva, who cruised past unranked Wang Cong at UFC 332 to capture the vacant women's flyweight title. Silva stays put at No. 2, however, below Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the title while recovering from injury.

Several other weight classes saw significant shifts, in some cases because of a lack of fights and in one case because of a fight booking for the future.

The most significant move is Alex Pereira shifting into the heavyweight rankings following the UFC's announcement that he will face Sergei Pavlovich on Dec. 12. It will be the second straight heavyweight fight for the former middleweight and light heavyweight champion, who has been No. 1 in the 205-pound rankings. He now moves to the heavyweight top 10, where he is ranked No. 7, two spots behind Pavlovich.

At light heavyweight, everyone previously below Pereira moves up, with ex-champion Magomed Ankalaev now No. 1. New to the top 10 are ninth-ranked Bogdan Guskov and No. 10 Robert Whittaker, as Khalil Rountree Jr. is out because he has not fought in over a year.

Also ineligible because of inactivity is middleweight Nassourdine Imavov, who is replaced in the 185-pound rankings by Christian Leroy Duncan. Perfect timing, as Duncan fights No. 5 Brendan Allen on Saturday's UFC card.

The other top-10 newcomer is men's bantamweight Payton Talbott, who knocked out Deiveson Figueiredo at UFC 332 to oust him from the rankings.

Here are the ESPN pound-for-pound MMA rankings and a list of current UFC champions in all weight classes.

Results are current; rankings as of Oct. 6. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

stories.headline: State of each position in 2026: What are the biggest tactical trends?
stories.summary: Elite soccer has changed dramatically in recent years, and the most valued player skill sets have evolved as a result.
stories.body:
Elite European soccer in 2026 feels decidedly different from what we've become used to. Over the past couple of seasons, the Premier League has been increasingly characterized by direct attacking, set pieces and long throw-ins. Many encounters between big clubs across Europe have become frenetic, end-to-end affairs, such as the Bayern Munich-Paris Saint-Germain semifinals in last season's UEFA Champions League.

A lot of the changes seem related to how teams play without the ball. The soccer we became accustomed to throughout the 2010s involved top sides trying to push their opponents back while keeping the ball. Once the ball reached the attacking third, they tried to outnumber defenders in key spaces and make use of their attacking talent.

One way for defensive sides to counter this approach is to use zonal marking, which involves defending space rather than individual players. They would set up in compact blocks and deny space in critical areas, whether they defended deep like Max Allegri's Juventus in the 2010s or pressed high like teams coached by Ralf Rangnick's disciples. While this tactic helps protect the areas closer to goal and prevent mismatches, it sometimes plays into the hands of those high-possession sides.

As a result, player marking (or man-to-man marking), in which defenders are assigned to follow attackers around up and down the pitch, started to make a comeback at the turn of the 2020s. Teams like Mikel Arteta's Arsenal and Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth combined this concept with their zonal marking, switching out of a zonal structure in certain situations to swarm teams attempting to move the ball forward (hybrid pressing). This makes moving the ball slowly up the pitch harder, causing teams to embrace more direct approaches with the ball.

Meanwhile, the game appears to be becoming more physical and more intense. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, every passing season of the Premier League has seen faster sprinting and more "high-intensity actions." And with off-ball physical data like running distance or top speed becoming more accessible, scouting departments now possess more transparent measures of athleticism, leading to players' athletic qualities being valued more.

Rather than just affecting the head coach's team talk, these big-picture changes have a major effect on the skill sets that clubs look for when assembling their starting XIs. Let's take a look at five positions -- goalkeepers, center backs, fullbacks, central midfielders, and strikers -- to see what has changed and why.

Goalkeepers: Distribution and cross-claiming

New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki has generated much buzz this season. One of his standout features has been his passing ability, playing quick passes to his center backs during the early buildup and exquisite floated long passes to Villa's forwards to escape pressure.

As impressive as his reflex saves are, Suzuki doesn't appear to be a great shot stopper. His "goals prevented" stats, based on post-shot expected goals, reveal that his shot-stopping numbers have hovered around that of the average major league goalkeeper over the past couple of seasons. In fact, in 2025-26, he prevented minus-0.4 goals per 90 minutes, implying that he did slightly worse than the average keeper last season.

However, his passing displays and his excellent cross-claiming make him a highly prized player, and his skill set epitomizes the state of today's goalkeeping.

When Pep Guardiola's Manchester City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma -- known for his shot-stopping abilities, but arguably an average distributor -- as their first-choice goalkeeper in summer 2025, it looked like elite soccer was once again prioritizing shot-stopping between the sticks. But the tactical conditions of soccer in the 2020s make ball-playing goalkeepers even more crucial than before; when teams are tasked with playing the ball past intense man-to-man presses, goalkeepers have more to do in the buildup phase.

Even the most aggressive man-to-man presses don't generally mark the goalkeeper, making keepers free options in the buildup. From this point, keepers are instrumental to playing quick passes around the box to try to bait the press for "artificial transitions" as well as with playing longer passes into space to relieve pressure and kick-start a direct attack.

As a result, the heyday of keepers primarily known for what they can do with their feet looks unlikely to recede anytime soon, with more intense pressing and more direct attacking arguably magnifying their value.

Meanwhile, although the number of open-play crosses that teams in the Big Five leagues play has decreased slightly since 2018, the ever-rising threat of set-play goals makes cross-claiming an especially valuable skill. The first-choice keepers at big clubs dominate the top of the leaderboard for cross-claiming statistics; Donnarumma ranked No. 1 for the highest percentage of crosses claimed in the Premier League last season, Barcelona's Joan García and Real Madrid's Thibaut Courtois ranked second and third, respectively, in last season's LaLiga campaign, and PSG's Lucas Chevalier ranked third in Ligue 1.

On the other hand, the keepers who populated the bottom of cross-claiming tables belong to either lower-table clubs or underperforming established sides like Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United. As valuable as goalkeepers' distribution is in 2026, it appears that the ability to claim crosses has become crucial to success between the sticks.

Center backs: Playmaking and pushing forward

In the 2015-16 Premier League season, the top five players who completed the most passes per 90 were Santi Cazorla, Cesc Fabregas, Bastian Schweinsteiger, Aaron Ramsey and Michael Carrick, with more central and attacking midfielders completing the top 10. In 2025-26, the top five were Rodri, Lewis Dunk, Curtis Jones, Trevoh Chalobah and William Saliba, with seven center backs making up the top 10.

A decade ago, central midfielders were at the heart of elite sides' passing moves, but today, especially in the Premier League, center backs are the primary passers in most sides.

In the Big Five leagues, center backs completed 19% more passes in the 2025-26 season than in 2018-19. Much of this has to do with intense man-to-man pressing systems, meaning that players positioned deeper have more prominent buildup duties. The 2020s have also seen nominal center backs become more involved in attacking play, taking up higher and wider positions. Attacking center backs are effective tools to dismantle mid-blocks, helping complicate marking duties with their movement.

This is easiest to do with wide center backs in a back three. Gian Piero Gasperini's Atalanta and Simone Inzaghi's Internazionale did this especially often. This season, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea and Gasperini's AS Roma are key examples, with the latter probably representing the most adventurous iteration of attacking center backs we've seen this century.

We can see some of this in back-four systems, too. Guardiola used John Stones as a center back who roved forward in possession at City, while Thiago Motta used Riccardo Calafiori and Jhon Lucumí as center backs with free roles.

As this decade progresses, the phrase "center back" might be encased in quotation marks more often.

Fullbacks: Rise of the underlap

Fullbacks often epitomize the tactical eras they find themselves in. The turn of the 2010s saw the rise of overlapping attacking fullbacks who move high up the pitch and outside wingers who cut inside with the ball. The mid-to-late 2010s saw the rise of high-intensity pressing, with high-possession sides using inverted fullbacks to provide security against counterattacks resulting from losing the ball. Meanwhile, the relative conservatism that followed the COVID-19 pandemic meant that nominal center backs were often deployed at fullback.

Today, we're seeing the rise of attacking fullbacks who underlap, making runs into the channels between opposition fullbacks and center backs, much like inverted wingers. As Caleb Gearty notes for SCOUTED, "the ability to receive the ball" is progressively becoming more highly valued for fullbacks. After getting in behind back lines, underlapping fullbacks can put in dangerous cutbacks and crosses from closer to goal, or take shots themselves.

In the case of back-three formations, this isn't a new phenomenon. For instance, Thomas Tuchel's Chelsea saw wingbacks Reece James and Ben Chilwell move inside and score goals, while Inzaghi used Federico Dimarco and Denzel Dumfries as goal-scoring threats at Inter.

But now, fullbacks in back-four systems are increasingly venturing forward and inside -- not just putting crosses in, but getting on the end of goal-scoring opportunities, too. Arsenal's Calafiori and Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly often make darting runs into the box and offer secondary goal threats. Spain's World Cup win saw Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro underlap, pulling defenses apart.

Meanwhile, back-three systems feature wingbacks who pose greater goal-scoring threats than ever. Alonso's Chelsea are an instructive example -- they signed Pep Chavarría and Marco Palestra, but Alonso currently appears to favor the left-footed winger Pedro Neto at right wingback, who makes sharp runs into the box.

Why is this the case? In an age when defensive tactics are dominated by player-marking, the positional interchanges around the flanks (or "wide rotations") and unexpected diagonal darts forward from fullbacks can scramble player-marking duties and open up space -- especially when wingers find themselves closer to the sideline. As Billy Carpenter writes, sudden moves into the spaces in behind defenses can expose structural vulnerabilities in even the best mid-blocks.

Calafiori so far this season represents a great example, making well-timed runs in behind and receiving incisive through balls ...

... and creating goals like these.

Jamie Carragher once remarked that fullbacks are either failed wingers or failed center backs. The rise of inverted fullbacks would've allowed Carragher to add "failed midfielder" to his jibe, while today, a middling inside forward can consider a successful career as an underlapping attacking fullback.

Central midfielders: Large spaces and generalists

In 2026, the most expensive player archetype to sign in soccer appears to be the generalist midfielder. Of the 10 most expensive transfers this summer per Transfermarkt, six were central midfielders. And among the major moves in midfield that big clubs made this summer, most midfielders are do-it-all generalists who, at least in theory, contribute to passing, carrying, winning the ball back and sometimes crashing the box. These include Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Bruno Guimarães, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

This hasn't always been the case. By 2009, the box-to-box midfielder had become a dying breed, superseded by specialists in midfield. In the late 2010s, the rise of pressing meant that press-resistant ball carriers in midfield became increasingly valued, epitomized by the summer 2019 transfer window, which saw Frenkie de Jong, Tanguy Ndombele and Mateo Kovacic move for sums exceeding €40 million. But now, every big club is willing to spend astronomic sums on their own equivalent of Declan Rice or Moisés Caicedo; athletic midfielders who can cover lots of ground and do a bit of everything.

Counterintuitively, this might be happening because less of the game is happening in midfield. With the rise of situational player-marking, the middle third sees larger spaces opened up between lines of pressure, while space becomes more constricted in teams' own thirds. As a result, moving the ball from defense to midfield becomes a harder task, while the spaces opened up in the middle third mean teams don't pass the ball around as much there, instead moving the ball through it more quickly.

Jon Mackenzie and Jake Entwistle have discussed the relevance of "small spaces" -- where the player on the ball has little room to work with in the face of pressure -- and "large spaces" -- where players need to cover ground quickly, especially during transitions or when a line of pressure is broken -- in midfield, which influences how midfielder profiles are valued today. A player like Anderson, who combines small-space and large-space skills, becomes priceless, but the broader emphasis shifts from small-space specialists to large-space generalists who can cover ground and offer control in the center of the park.

As a result, affecting the pace of the attack, rather than just exerting control over space, becomes a key consideration in midfield. The rise of artificial transitions in response to pressing also means central midfielders are key to moving the ball from small spaces to large spaces, as Carlos Baleba did adeptly while at Brighton.

The middle of the park is integral to controlling a game of soccer, and as we're seeing the very notion of "control" change in the middle of the 2020s, the traits associated with the most highly valued midfielders are transformed, too.

Strikers: Physicality and pinning

While the first two decades of top-level soccer in the 21st century saw increasing versatility at the center forward position, the opposite is happening in the third decade. So far, the 2020s have seen taller, faster and stronger strikers being valued more than their smaller, more technical counterparts. Of course, Erling Haaland represents the platonic ideal of a striker -- in this era and in any other -- but the players who spearhead attacks in the middle of the 2020s tend to be 6-foot-2 or taller, and combine their size with pace.

Today's strikers are also less involved in link-up play than their equivalents at the turn of the 2020s, with the average striker in the Big Five leagues completing 16% fewer passes in 2025-26 than in 2018-19.

As discussed earlier, with attacks becoming more direct, the established strategy of pushing teams back and overwhelming defenses with patient play in the attacking third is falling out of fashion, which means strikers don't need to be as involved outside the penalty area. Instead, strikers increasingly spend most of the game pinning back defenders and stretching back lines, attempting to find space within settled defensive blocks. Plus, an increased emphasis on transitions correspondingly makes outlets to hit on the break becoming more valuable, and some extra size certainly comes in handy while trying to score goals from set pieces.

However, the players who currently lead most big clubs' front lines indicate the trend might be reversing at the upper echelons of the game. Harry Kane drops deeper than ever and conducts passing moves from midfield at Bayern, PSG won the Champions League with Ousmane Dembélé as a false 9 last season, Mikel Arteta appears to favor Kai Havertz up front over Viktor Gyokeres at Arsenal, and Barcelona currently deploy Raphinha at the No. 9 spot.

This might be because teams are finding alternate ways of manipulating player-marking strategies, picking holes in defenses with positional interchanges. By dropping deeper, a striker can bring the defender assigned to marking him along and create space for teammates. For example, in this case, João Pedro dropping deep to receive a throw-in pokes a hole for Morgan Rogers to run into, who in turn creates space for Cole Palmer's carry and goal.

For now, specialized, physically gifted strikers may have their time in the sun, but we're likely to see many approaches at the center forward position as the decade progresses.

What to make of 2026 trends

Many soccer fans view today's tactical landscape as being one of stasis or even regression. It's tempting to view the rise of directness and set pieces, as well as do-it-all midfielders and big strikers, as the return of older approaches. But this might be a reductive view; as Mackenzie notes in his book "The Spectre of Pep," presenting changes in the tactical landscape as purely being "cyclical" makes it "very difficult to speak of the 'new' in any meaningful way at all."

All the smaller tactical shifts we're seeing across the pitch are happening in relation to broader changes in the tactical environment of the 2020s. With the rise of man-to-man pressing approaches and the resulting revival of direct attacking, accompanied with the resurgence of ground-eating midfielders and big, physical strikers, these very same trends have brought about the rise of playmaking goalkeepers, attacking center backs, and underlapping fullbacks.

If a Premier League manager from 2006 drove a plutonium-powered DeLorean to 2026, he might find the first five minutes of play recognizable, but would be scandalized by the time he reaches the 10-minute mark. Welcome to elite soccer in the 2020s.

stories.headline: October Draft Power Rankings: Extended top 40 in the post-Combine rankings
stories.summary: There's movement in the top 10 after the AFL Draft's national Combine. Here's Jasper Chellappah's October Power Rankings, with an extended top 40 prospects ranked.
stories.body:
The final opportunity for prospects to elevate their draft stock was on show at the AFL Draft Combine. Through athletic testing there were risers and sliders, but even more importantly was the opportunity for clubs to meet face to face and properly evaluate the talent in the 2026 draft crop.

The overwhelming consensus from recruiters is that this year's crop runs deeper than the 2025 edition. Clubs will be more confident picking through the second round and into the third, which is reflected in the value of those selections at the trade table.

With rule changes, you can expect a much shorter first round with higher picks required to match early bids. That's despite the top two talents in the draft being club-tied and a further two to three being snapped up in the first round. There could be as little as 18 to 20 selections on the first night of the draft in direct contrast to the 25 and 27 players taken in the previous two drafts.

As opposed to last year when Willem Duursma separated himself as the pick 1 apparent, there is no concrete news on which way Essendon is heading in the open pool. A group of five leading prospects are all still genuine chances despite the buzz around a Vic Country midfielder. Port Adelaide NGA star Dougie Cochrane is all but assured of having his name read out first come November 19th.

These top 40 draft rankings reflect where prospects are expected to be taken based on exposed form, upside at AFL level and club intel after a week where every recruiting team gets together and consolidates draft boards.

Just six weeks out from the 2026 AFL Draft, this is ESPN's post-combine power rankings for October.

Full combine wrap and results here
Previous rankings: April | May | June | July | August | September | October

1. Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide NGA) (previously: 1)

Central District/South Australia

FWD/MID, 195cm

SANFL: 4 games, 17.8 disposals, 3.8 marks, 2.3 tackles

Cochrane has stuck at one all season long despite only playing four games at the tail end of 2026. The Port NGA gun has sat at the top of the crop since his exploits in the U16s national championships. In his return to the SANFL he played in defence, taking kick ins and collecting gaudy numbers in trying conditions at times. He's a do-it-all tall with elite aerial prowess, strong running numbers and a booming kick. Cochrane will be drafted at no. 1 by Port Adelaide through a matched bid, and the key forward possesses midfield ambitions in time.

Traits similar to: Charlie Curnow

2. Cody Walker (Carlton father-son) (2)

Bendigo Pioneers/Vic Country

MID, 184cm

National Championships: 3 games, 23.7 disposals, 3.7 clearances, 1.3 tackles

Walker is one of the more impressive footballers to come through the pathways in some time. He's effectively been part of the Carlton squad while playing in the VFL side this year, attending line meetings and team dinners while living full-time in Melbourne. The Echuca native is a natural ball-winner and excellent athlete with fast twitch lateral movement through congestion. He breaks tackles, drives his legs and showed his aerobic power with a 6:04 minute 2km at the combine. Walker's knocks have, and continue to be, his ball use and decision making. He bites off a lot on most of his touches and his rushed disposal can be detrimental at times.

Traits similar to: Chad Warner

3. Arki Butler (3)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 182cm

National Championships: 3 games, 12.3 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.7 goals

Butler's season was impacted by a cracked collarbone at the championships and a hamstring that ruled him out of combine testing. That all came after some of the biggest performances you'll see this year. Butler had a game of 33 disposals, eight goals and seven behinds for Brighton Grammar, and a 26-disposal, four-goal outing in Sandringham's opening game this year. He's powerfully built and thrives in one-on-ones ahead of the ball where his strong hands in the air and speed off the mark at ground level sees him kick goals in a variety of ways. It will take a brave team to read out Butler's name in the top three of this draft given his position as a small forward and late-season injuries, but it may take an even braver team to pass up the most high-impact player in this year's draft.

Traits similar to: Toby Greene

READ: 'All damage' - Arki Butler is the 2026 draft's most watchable junior footballer

4. Ethan Drever (6)

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

MID, 188cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 4.2 tackles

Coming into the season Drever loomed as a potential first round prospect. He's now the most likely to have his name read out first in the open pool. Drever is the ideal modern day midfielder, with leg-driving burst out of the front of stoppage and a penchant for kicking long-range goals. He has a want to chase and pressure that comes through in his tackle numbers, and has put together consistent performances in wins and losses across an injury-free year. It's all come together for the Ballarat local to potentially be Essendon's choice at the top of the board.

Traits similar to: Finn Callaghan

5. Harry Van Hattum (5)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

RUC/FWD, 205cm

National Championships: 4 games, 10.8 disposals, 2.5 marks, 22.0 hitouts

There hasn't been a prospect quite like Van Hattum to come through the draft in decades. Rucks have been drafted this high in recent years, but not possessing the mature body and physicality that defines Van Hattum's game. He's an enforcer through the middle of the ground and loves to follow up with strength through the contest. On the outside the Knights star is a beautiful kick on his preferred right and has scope to be a genuine goalkicker in the forward 50. Inconsistency and concerns over his ability to cover the ground means Van Hattum has dropped from pick one contention, but he's a probable top 10 pick and has all the talent in the world to become the next great ruckman in the AFL.

Traits similar to: Brodie Grundy

READ: 'I just hate that' - Harry Van Hattum wants to end ruck disrespect

6. Heath Mellody (4)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID/DEF, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 28.2 disposals, 5.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Larke Medal, All-Australian captain, WAFL Grand Final. It was a magnificent finish to 2026 for Mellody, who has risen into pick one calculations following a league debut that was undeniable. The hard-running Claremont product graduated on-ball for WA and starred with big numbers and a balanced style, blending inside grunt work with elite spread. His kicking suffered under pressure but it's one of his weapons streaming off halfback so recruiters won't be concerned with his inefficiency through the midfield, and he showed he can mix it with senior bodies. Mellody will be right in the mix for West Coast's pick three come November and won't be available much later given his exposed form, though he clearly ran out of steam towards the end of the season and wasn't a standout at the combine with a 6:30 minute 2km and 3.042 second 20m sprint.

Traits similar to: Lachie Ash

7. Gus Teixeira (5)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.0 disposals, 4.2 tackles, 1.8 goals

The power, composure and skill Teixeira plays with gives him a great platform to explode at the next level. There's little doubt he can become a midfielder but his best football for Vic Metro came as a half forward where he took the game on and hit the scoreboard consistently. Teixeira doesn't have the tricks of the game's best small forwards but he plays with the aggression befitting the most damaging mid-forwards in the AFL. His draft range is entrenched in the top 10.

Traits similar to: Jordan De Goey

8. Sam Gayfer (13)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

FWD, 194cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.0 disposals, 4.2 marks, 2.5 goals

The biggest riser out of the weekend, but not just through his testing. Gayfer is an elite athletic prospect with the highest leap of any prospect to test at the national combine. It comes through in the tape; Gayfer took one of the great hangers out of the goal square earlier in the year, a moment that will be replayed throughout his career. He's become the leading key forward prospect and was a talisman for Vic Metro's undefeated campaign, plus impressed in club interviews and with his attitude towards his footy future. The nephew of Collingwood premiership defender Mick, Gayfer is right in the sights of the Pies and Saints at the end of the top 10, and could even be a consideration for North Melbourne and Melbourne earlier in the piece.

Traits similar to: Mitch Georgiades

9. Mitch Harris (8)

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 8.8 disposals, 3.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Amongst a crop of three excellent key defensive prospects this year Harris has separated himself. He played impressively at league level for WWT including three finals outings, but didn't test at the combine after an ankle injury playing basketball the week prior. Clubs know that Harris is an old school lockdown defender that rarely gets beaten, but are keen to see him take on more responsibility intercepting in the air and even make good on opportunities forward of the ball. Harris values defence highly and has the size to take on genuine key forwards at the next level.

Traits similar to: Sam Collins

10. Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) (9)

Giants Academy/Allies

MID, 186cm

National Championships: 2 games, 25.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 6.0 tackles

Matthews has been out of sight since a blistering start to the national championships for the Allies, but the Giants know they have their best academy prospect since Tom Green. He's a balanced midfielder with elite hands in the contest and the want to spread and link up in transition. GWS is in an interesting spot with a bid expected around their pick seven on draft night - they could find more points and trade up to snare two top 10 talents, or even take him with their live selection.

Traits similar to: Sam Flanders

11. Wil Malady (10)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.7 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.3 goals

Malady had a litany of brilliant moments late in the season. For Caulfield Grammar in the APS Grand Final he was a clear standout for his side in a losing effort, and he ripped the Talent League Grand Final apart with a flurry of goals in the third term. His excellent aerial craft is aided by a monster leap and he has the speed and agility to wow at ground level. Malady plays a difficult role as a third tall that can also start on a wing, but he makes his moments count and possesses all the tools to become an impactful forward at the next level.

Traits similar to: Ollie Henry

12. Clancy Snell (11)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 196cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 7.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Snell is the best intercept mark in the pool. An excellent reader of the play that backs himself to roll off his man and kickstart transition, there have been moments where it can backfire and his direct opponent gets off the chain. It's a style of play that can suit the modern game but Snell hasn't convinced clubs he can be more disciplined in his defending. He ran a strong 6:23 minute 2km in a sign he can get involved offensively up field and there's little doubt he will become a weapon out of the backline, but the concerns around his capacity to defend one-on-one are real.

Traits similar to: Josh Worrell

13. Leo Steed (14)

Swan Districts/Western Australia

MID, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 23.5 disposals, 3.0 marks, 4.0 tackles

Steed isn't the most naturally gifted footballer but he gets the absolute best out of himself. Over the off-season he transformed his kicking action and has become a reliable ball user, and his engine was on show all year as a pure midfielder at colts level and for WA. At league level he played heavy forward minutes and was able to impact, but there are concerns around his positional versatility at the next level. Steed's clean hands, dogged defensive running and professionalism will see him taken in the first round with hopes that he makes it as a genuine inside midfielder despite his size.

Traits similar to: Caleb Serong

14. Caylen Murray (Lions Academy) (17)

Lions Academy/Allies

DEF/MID, 183cm

National Championships: 4 games, 24.0 disposals, 6.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

There's a real chance that Lions Academy star Murray is a top 10 pick in November. That would put a significant points crunch on Brisbane with a 20% Grand Final loading meaning they would need to find an additional first round pick for the Allies MVP. Offering silky ball use and smooth movement out of the backline, Murray looks an excellent halfback option in the crop. He works hard to the right spots and is reliable by hand and foot, plus has provided flashes of upside as a centre bounce midfielder. Clubs are keen on the Maroochydore product who knows his future may not be with the Lions.

Traits similar to: Lachie Whitfield

15. Jake Eime (15)

Central District/South Australia

DEF, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 1.2 tackles

The speed that Eime plays with plus his penchant to take the game on and break lines gives him a great chance at being a first round pick. He recorded a 6:12 minute 2km and 3.001 second 20m sprint in a showing of his athleticism on the weekend. The Crows were knocked back in their bid to have him added to their NGA program this year, but would be right in the mix for him in the first round regardless.

Traits similar to: Darcy Wilmot

16. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) (12)

FWD, 174cm

National Championships: 1 game, 10.0 disposals, 5.0 tackles, 1.0 goals

El Souki just kept kicking goals and making defenders look silly. A natural footballer with the power to play through contact, the Dogs NGA product is a lovely left foot user and has enjoyed successful midfield minutes across the season. He's worked hard on his fitness and ball skills to prove to recruiters he can step into a professional environment and thrive.

Traits similar to: Kysaiah Pickett

READ: 'They'd follow me knowing I kick goals' - NGA-tied Khaled El Souki is in first-round contention

17. Jack Pickett (23)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

FWD, 194cm

Clubs haven't forgotten that Pickett was the leading key forward prospect heading into the season. Unfortunately he tore his ACL before playing a game and has been rehabilitating it ever since. Pickett has presence down the line, playing at his best with hands outstretched on the lead. He's an accurate set shot and kicked 31 goals from eight games last year.

Traits similar to: Jye Amiss

18. Tyson Bradley (20)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 14.5 disposals, 6.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Bradley is the third key defender in the first round mix. He's the best ball user of the group and has been a leader through his junior career, plus took out Vic Metro's MVP in an undefeated championships. Concerns around his athleticism may be warranted, but Bradley also recorded a top 10 time in the agility test this weekend. He will need to add size through pre-seasons before taking on the AFL's key forwards.

Traits similar to: Jordan Ridley

19. Koby LeCras (26)

West Perth/Western Australia

FWD/MID, 192cm

LeCras partially tore his ACL after a best on ground performance for the AFL Academy. Six months on and he took part in the 2km, posting a 6:23 despite only training fully for six weeks. It was an impressive return and showed his diligence in rehab. LeCras can play on a wing or through the forward line, seeing himself as a third tall that can kick goals in a variety of ways. The nephew of Eagles premiership small forward Mark deserves consideration towards the back end of the first round.

Traits similar to: Ollie Dempsey

20. Ethan Herbert (18)

North Adelaide/South Australia

RUC/FWD, 200cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.8 disposals, 3.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Herbert operates as another midfielder when the ball hits the deck with good hands below his knees and an appetite to spread and be an option around the ground. Clubs also see upside in him at either end of the ground. He doesn't have great ruck craft and has been beaten by others at times this year, but his strengths are encouraging and there's real upside in his game at senior level with time.

Traits similar to: Tim English

21. Kodah Edwards (19)

South Adelaide/South Australia

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 4 games, 22.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 3.2 tackles

Edwards's positional versatility will help him come November. The SA captain was a beacon of consistency at the championships in a tough year for the Croweaters and put up massive numbers in the SANFL U18s. He's a contested midfielder first and foremost, but has had great success winning one-on-ones and kicking goals up forward. Edwards's lack of pace and haphazard kicking are the main concerns going into the draft.

Traits similar to: Matt Kennedy

22. Noah Williams (21)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

MID, 177cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.5 disposals, 4.0 marks, 5.8 tackles

Williams has slid this year after a hot start for the Falcons and AFL Academy. He's a smaller midfielder that doesn't use the ball particularly well, but his tackling pressure and endeavour to play defence is a highlight. Williams works himself into the ground and if not for a torrid stretch of injuries he would have shown more in his top-age campaign.

Traits similar to: Tom Atkins

23. Harvie Cooke (25)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.5 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.0 goals

Cooke couldn't have done much more this year. He took out the Talent League best and fairest and showed he can play good football as a forward when required for Vic Metro. He's clean and quick to process the game around him, moving the ball at tempo. Preventing him from moving up the board is doubts about his midfield proficiency given his size and lack of standout athletic traits.

Traits similar to: Jake Soligo

24. Toby Krasna (28)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 3 games, 19.0 disposals, 3.3 marks, 1.0 goals

Krasna has fans in the first round. There's some X-factor in his forward-half game, able to zig and zag around opponents while picking out teammates further afield with neat ball skills. If he doesn't stick as a midfielder at the next level it may be difficult for him to impact off half forward after a season where he was at his best with heavy on-ball clock.

Traits similar to: Jake Soligo

25. Marlon Neocleous (22)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD/MID, 168cm

National Championships: 2 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 0.5 goals

There's no doubting Neocleous has the tricks befitting the game's best small forwards. He looks up to Nick Watson and similarly has some extraordinary moments that catch the eye, but he doesn't possess the pace to separate from the best lockdown defenders which limits his upside. Neocleous loves to get up the ground and is incisive with his ball use.

Traits similar to: Jack Higgins

26. Harrison Chapman (16)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 18.7 disposals, 4.7 marks, 2.0 tackles

Chapman will likely slide on draft night in comparison to the talent he possesses after an inconsistent season. He can play a variety of roles and as of now looks most at home on a wing where he can work in space because of his skinny frame limiting the contested ball he wins. If he can put the running, class and ball use together while adding to his frame there's real upside in what he presents as a midfielder in time.

Traits similar to: Will Day

27. Gabe Patterson (24)

Glenelg/South Australia

FWD, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 2.5 tackles, 1.0 goals

Patterson has been difficult to place in the overall rankings for clubs. The forward ran a 7:05 minute 2km and was trailing his group, but is clearly a burst athlete with the power to win his own ball. Patterson has had massive games including a five goal outing late in the season but has also been inconsistent and didn't impact at the championships. Clubs know his talent is worthy of a first round pick.

Traits similar to: Beau McCreery

28. Keenan Boi (Hawthorn NGA) (29)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 180cm

National Championships: 3 games, 13.3 disposals, 4.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Boi is a cult hero in waiting - the attack on the man and ball, flowing locks and forward-half power all stand out when you watch him in action, but there's a steeliness to his game that will ensure he can transition up a level. Boi can play a variety of selfless roles as a medium forward and makes quick decisions under pressure that are typically good.

Traits similar to: Sam Powell-Pepper

29. Lochie Burrows (33)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF/MID, 181cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 4.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

There are clubs who rate Burrows as a first round pick this year. The hard-nosed midfielder played some of his best footy as a defender at the national championships and showed off his versatility through all three areas of the ground. He runs hard, competes defensively and gets his hands dirty, but may be pigeonholed into lockdown defensive roles in the AFL.

Traits similar to: Max Michalanney

30. Albert MacGowan (31)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 187cm

National Championships: 4 games, 22.8 disposals, 6.2 marks, 1.0 tackles

MacGowan led all comers in the 2km time trial in a stellar 5:59 minutes. That engine is on show through games off a wing and in minutes on-ball he's held his own too. The questions remain around his pace at the next level, but MacGowan's overhead marking, footy IQ and running power will give him a chance of becoming a good wingman.

Traits similar to: Matt Johnson

31. George Dimer (30)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

FWD, 173cm

National Championships: 3 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Dimer is full of energy and creativity, always on the move at stoppages and at the drop of the ball, ready to impact with clean hands and a turn of pace. He offers good forward craft and can use his size advantageously to draw free kicks or flash through packs and emerge with ball in hand.

Traits similar to: Hussien El Achkar

32. Sam Devers (-)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

DEF, 189cm

National Championships: 2 games, 12.0 disposals, 2.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Devers tested well at the combine and is in that second round frame for some clubs. He ran a blistering 2.925 20m sprint which comes across in his willingness to tuck the ball and run out of defence. He can be scrappy by foot but the size to play on a range of forwards and attacking mindset shines through in-game.

Traits similar to: Tom McCarthy

33. George Gale (35)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 27.8 disposals, 5.2 marks, 2.8 tackles

Gale was an inside beast for WA this season and finished his year in a WAFL Grand Final with Claremont. Showing he matched up with senior bodies was important, but his lack of pace will be a detriment in the AFL system. Gale is professional, competes hard and is a good kick in space so could stick as a wingman.

Traits similar to: Bo Allan

34. Darcy Szerszyn (-)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

DEF, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.8 disposals, 5.0 marks, 1.0 tackles

Szerszyn had a strong combine and that comes across in the tape, with speed off the mark and a good leap at his size. He has matched up on key forwards in the past but will be a third tall option at the next level with the want to run and carry off halfback, and can be entrusted as a ball user out of defence.

Traits similar to: Bodhi Uwland

35. Lachie Hicks (-)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 16.8 disposals, 4.5 marks, 2.0 tackles

Possibly the biggest winner out of the combine was Hicks. He went fifth all-time in the agility test, ran the second best 2km and was top 10 in the sprint. Hicks is a ball magnet through the midfield with elite spread from congestion, but needs to become a better ball user and make better decisions in dangerous areas to warrant on-ball minutes.

Traits similar to: Joe Richards

36. Jackson Phillips (27)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

MID, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 3.2 tackles

Phillips's Stingrays are Grand Final bound, aided by his excellent midfield play. He offers impact with every possession, not collecting huge numbers but getting the ball in dangerous spots and regularly hitting the scoreboard. He likely doesn't exhibit the tools to be a bona fide inside midfielder at the next level but has positional versatility in his ball use and running power and could play off a wing or half forward.

Traits similar to: Brayden Cook

37. Marcus Prasad (32)

Dandenong Stingrays

FWD/MID, 167cm

Talent League: 10 games, 18.6 disposals, 4.8 tackles, 2.0 goals

Prasad didn't garner enough interest to attend the national combine but he has some serious traits. The small forward gets up the ground to impact and has fantastic hands under pressure, executing skills quickly and stepping out of trouble with composure. His size means he'll be limited to the inside 50 but Prasad's agility and quickness hand to foot is an intriguing mix.

Traits similar to: Isaiah Dudley

38. Xavier Ladbrook (-)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 201cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.5 disposals, 5.5 marks, 0.8 goals

Rated as the fourth key defender in the draft class, Ladbrook is a good runner that has spent time up on a wing or roaming forward as well. He plays within himself with safe ball use and doesn't have the intercepting prowess of Power teammate Snell but offers interesting traits for teams to invest in with the running power at his height. He will need to build size to play down back in the future.

Traits similar to: Ethan Read

39. Benji Van Rooyen (35)

Claremont/Western Australia

RUC, 203cm

National Championships: 4 games, 14.0 disposals, 4.0 marks, 20.5 hitouts

Van Rooyen was the best performing ruck at the national championships. Working against him is the time he may take to develop his conditioning and aerial presence on an AFL list. He's a competitor that, while lacking brother Jacob's athleticism, has safe hands and a selflessness that works alongside his midfielders.

Traits similar to: Jordon Sweet

40. Cody Templeton (-)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 180cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.3 disposals, 1.3 tackles, 1.7 goals

Templeton didn't earn a national combine invite but it didn't stop him from ripping apart the Talent League Grand Final in a reminder of his skillset. The powerful forward can be a difficult matchup; always on the move and able to separate quickly, Templeton kicked five goals from 18 disposals to propel Gippsland to the premiership. His draft range may not begin much earlier than this point but he should get an opportunity on an AFL list.

Traits similar to: Ben Long

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
